lines.note: Sanyacu is defined simply as a certain medicine. The initial S is a capital matching the other headwords, not the OCR's lowercase letter; Hũa retains its nasal abbreviation. This entry also confirms the preceding page's separate San- catchword.

Yama cague means mountain shade, matching the Portuguese sombra dos montes. The terminal written-language label is upright; no separate point is securely visible after this S, unlike the pointed label on the next line.

Yamano ſaru means a mountain or woodland monkey, agreeing with bugio dos matos. The long s belongs to the Japanese gloss and the final S. is an upright usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese sentence.
Sanyet is equated with Mairu, “go or come.” The bare final t is retained rather than expanded, and i, remains roman with the Japanese synonym; only the Portuguese definition is italic.

The entry concerns reckoning and accounts. The initial S omitted by OCR is visible, and the example begins Sã- with a nasal mark and a true line-end hyphen, not a period. Cangaye mochijru is retained in its printed spelling rather than silently rewriting the Japanese paraphrase.
Completes Sãyô ſuru across the preceding break and explains it as counting or making accounts. The initial fragment remains on this physical line; the circumflex and long s are visible.
Mitçuno tomo means three companions, matching the Portuguese. The headword has a caron over u, and the Portuguese companheiros visibly divides after companhei-.
Completes companheiros, “companions,” from the preceding line. The separate upright S. marks written usage; it should not remain inside the italic continuation merely because it shares the short row.

runs.text: Couſa mal feita, fea, ou que ſocede o

lines.note: Sanzan describes something badly done, ugly, or going badly. The final isolated o is visible before the next line's mal; the awkward Portuguese wording is retained rather than grammatically repaired. Fea also remains in its historical spelling.

Finishes the preceding definition with “badly/ill, etc.” The short continuation is not a separate sense or headword, and the potentially awkward preceding o is a source reading rather than a reason to change this row.
Sanzanna gives the adjectival form of Sanzan and refers back to the same meaning. The initial capital S lost by OCR is present; the grammatical label and Latin Idem belong to the italic apparatus.
Sanzanni is the corresponding adverbial form. The abbreviated grammatical label is italic, and the double n is meaningful morphology consistent with the immediately preceding adjectival entry.
Yamano ſô identifies monks living in the mountains. Portuguese Bonzos supplies that religious sense, and morão retains the printed nasal ending; the location continues on the next row.
Completes the monks' location, “in the mountains.” This single italic word belongs to Sanzô and is retained as a physical continuation rather than combined with the next entry.
The Japanese explanations mean a mountain thief or bandit. Nuſubito retains its long s, and Yamadachi is an alternative introduced by i,; neither synonym is an embedded term within Portuguese prose.

runs.text: Ladrão dos matos, ou ſalteador de caminhos.

lines.note: The Portuguese confirms the preceding Japanese gloss as a woodland thief or highway robber. The long s in ſalteador and the italic run are visible; no additional Japanese material starts on this line.
Mitçuno michi means three paths; the Portuguese begins a description of three paths of torment. The doubled zz belongs to the historical headword spelling and is not simplified.

runs.text: tormentos por onde paßão os que vão ao inferno.

lines.note: The preceding paths are described as routes of torment traversed by those going to hell. This is the dictionary's religious explanation, not a modern doctrinal expansion. The double-s sort in paßão and the tilde in vão are retained.

A separate Sanzzu denotes a horse's haunches. The identical headword spelling does not connect this anatomical sense to the preceding religious entry; the Portuguese caualo retains historical u for v.

runs.text: Aduerb. Modo de eſpalhar, ou de ſe

lines.note: Sappato is an adverb of thorough scattering or clearing away. The scan reads a after S, correcting Sippato; the Portuguese syntax continues after de ſe, so this row does not finish the definition.
The definition continues with shaking off or washing completely, then begins the example Sappato natta. The Japanese past form physically divides at nat-; the terminal hyphen is visible.

runs.text: Ficar limpo, & lauado de toda a immũ

lines.note: Completes natta and explains becoming completely clean and washed of all dirt. The scan resolves limpo and the single word lauado, correcting OCR limoo and laua do. The nasal abbreviation immũ ends the row without a securely visible hyphen.

runs.text: dicia. Itẽ, Ficar cõ todo o fato perdido no fogo,

lines.note: Completes immũdicia, then adds the figurative situation of having all one's belongings lost in a fire. The abbreviations Itẽ and cõ are retained, and fato here concerns possessions or effects rather than the modern English “fact.”

The next example means scattering things completely. Enlargement shows the faint stem and hooked head of ſ between a and u in torichiraſu; the apparently floating mark is not a tilde on u. This restores the verb missed by OCR, with the worn sort remaining a nonblocking caveat.

runs.text: por cà, & por acolà algũa couſa ſem ordem.

lines.note: Completes the scattering example as spreading something here and there without order. The two location words have grave accents, whereas algũa carries a nasal tilde; those different marks are not interchangeable.

Sappǔqeina fito describes an unceremonious or curt person. Both the headword and example have the same Sappǔqei stem, correcting the OCR's broken Sapi ǔiqeina. The Portuguese begins Homẽ, retaining its abbreviated final nasal.

runs.text: ſeco de palauras, & de poucos comprimentos.

lines.note: The person is “dry in words” and sparing in courtesies. Printed comprimentos is retained despite the modern distinction from cumprimentos; the Portuguese meaning corroborates the curt-person example rather than a literal length measurement.
Saqe denotes the drink here called vinho. The causative nomaſuru introduces giving someone drink; its long s is integral to the Japanese form. The explanation starts with Dar and continues below.
Finishes “give to drink” and introduces urging someone to drink. The Japanese ſuſumuru retains both long-s positions, and the Portuguese verb persuadir physically divides after Perſua-.
Completes persuading someone to drink, then gives Saqeni yô for being affected by drink. The circumflex over yô is visible; the following Portuguese state description continues on the next row.
The previous example means being touched or overcome by wine. A new Japanese example begins with Saqeni at the end of the same row; it is not part of the italic Portuguese wording.

Completes Saqeni chozuru and gives fitaru as an alternative, glossed as being soaked in wine. Enlargement supports the faint initial f and intervening t in fitaru, rather than OCR ſiaru; these damaged strokes remain a nonblocking caveat. No accent is securely printed on the final u of chozuru.
Finishes the preceding description, “soaked in wine.” This single word belongs to the Japanese drinking example above, not to the separate fish entry that follows.

This Saqe is a fish name, with Saqeno iuo as an alternative. The Portuguese compares it with another fish on the next row; l, is the roman alternative marker. Second-pass enlargement shows a two-stroke final n in Hun, unlike the wider m in nearby como; the printed form is retained rather than regularized to Hum.
Completes the comparison with salmon, printed ſarmão. The historical r-spelling and the nasal mark are retained rather than normalized to salmão.

The verb entry first gives tearing, then begins Youo ſaquru, a separate example concerning withdrawal from the world. The principal parts uru and eta remain literal, and the example visibly divides at ſa-.

runs.text: Dar de mão, ou deſprezar o mundo.

lines.note: Completes Youo ſaquru and explains renouncing or despising the world. The phrase dar de mão is part of the historical Portuguese idiom; it is not replaced with a modern paraphrase in the canonical text.

Nanuo ſaquru means avoiding danger, matching the Portuguese withdrawal or escape. The printed eſcapar- ends with a hyphen; the next line starts directly with de, so an expected reflexive ſe must not be invented.

Completes the danger-avoidance explanation, “from dangers.” The short continuation contains no visible ſe before de; the resulting Portuguese irregularity is preserved as printed, not silently repaired.

The principal parts identify the verb for shouting, crying out, or lamenting. The past ending ôda and the nasal abbreviation in prãtear are visible; neither is modernized to a contemporary inflection or spelling.
The noun Saqebi gives a cry, shout, or lament, following the verb's corresponding senses. The Portuguese pranto is written out here rather than using the preceding row's nasal abbreviation.

This names a raw-fish preparation associated with the salmon's head. Enlargement resolves the damaged fizzunamaſu, including the doubled z and final long s, rather than the OCR's fizana naſu; the rubbed middle strokes remain a minor caveat. The supplied NINJAL entry corroborates the word identity, not its allographs. The Portuguese begins “a certain fish dish.”

runs.text: crù, que ſe faz da cabeça de hum certo peixe

lines.note: The dish is made raw from the head of a certain fish. The scan reads crù, not OCR erù, and hum, not ham; the grave accent is retained and the comparison with salmon follows below.
Completes the description with a fish like salmon. The spelling ſarmão agrees with the earlier fish definition on this page, preserving its r and nasal ending.
Saqeno iuo redirects to Saqe. The headword begins S, correcting OCR F; the italic Vide is an editorial cross-reference, while the referenced Japanese Saqe is upright within that apparatus.
Saqenomi means a drinker, matching Portuguese bebedor de vinho. The second b in Bebedor is visible and corrects OCR Behedor; the entry is distinct from the rice-related homograph immediately below.

runs.text: Arroz que eſtà ja conuertido em

lines.note: This Saqenomi concerns rice already converted into the drink. The scan restores the same headword spelling, correcting Baqeromi, and resolves conuertido rather than comertido. The small real space in eſtà ja is retained, with no added accent on ja.
Completes “rice already converted into wine.” The word is visibly indented as a continuation, so its placement has been changed from flush-left to indented without changing the line ID or crop.
Saqeno yoi describes drunkenness or a drunken person, here glossed simply Bebado. The Portuguese is unaccented in the print; an expected modern accent is not added.
The compound verb means becoming torn or breaking apart by tearing. The principal parts ru and eta are preserved, and both Portuguese long-s forms belong to the italic definition.
Introduces an example about trousers becoming badly opened or torn at the seams. The printed vô has a circumflex, Vt is italic, and the compound's second element visibly breaks at yabu-.

Completes yabureta, followed by the upright source citation Mon. The Portuguese says that the trousers tore; its close printed calçoensſe is retained without inserting a modern word space. Mon. is a citation label, not part of the Japanese sentence.
Completes the cited translation with the trousers breaking apart greatly. Enlargement confirms the narrow e in romperão, so no apparent contracted romprão reading is adopted.
This verb entry means flowering. Fanaga ſaqu begins the example “the flowers bloom”; the historical principal part aita is retained rather than replaced by a modernized form.

runs.text: Sairem, ou começarem a abrir as flores.

lines.note: Completes Fanaga ſaqu and explains flowers coming out or beginning to open. The physical split is inside the Japanese verb, while the rest of the row is an italic Portuguese explanation.

A homographic verb means tearing or opening through the middle, distinct from flowering. The aligned short s in Rasgar and the historical pollo meo are retained as printed rather than harmonized with neighbouring long-s spellings.
Cuchiuo ſaqu means tearing the mouth open, followed by the start of a lightning example. The Portuguese aboca is visibly close-joined and remains so; Rai- has a true terminal hyphen.
Completes Raiqua vochite qiuo ſaita, describing lightning falling and splitting a tree. The q in qiuo and the historical past ſaita agree with the tearing verb; the Portuguese begins the same event.

runs.text: abrio, & fendeo hũa aruore, ou pao.

lines.note: The lightning opened and split a tree or piece of wood. The abbreviation hũa and historical abrio, fendeo and pao remain literal. A new Japanese example begins To- at the row's end without an inserted paragraph sign.
Completes Toriuo ſaqu, “split or carve a bird.” The enlarged scan supports the close join outrinchar; the Portuguese bird word divides after paßa-, with its double-s sort retained.

runs.text: ro: mas particularmente ſe entende da galinha

lines.note: Completes paßaro and qualifies that the expression particularly concerns a kind of game bird. The enlarged scan reveals a colon after ro, omitted by OCR; the qualification continues into the next row.
Completes galinha do mato, the game-bird qualification attached to Toriuo ſaqu. The short italic row does not introduce an independent bird-name entry.
Saqi means the point or tip of something. The scan supports the unusual quelquer rather than a normalized qualquer; that source spelling is preserved while the sense remains straightforward.
This Saqi concerns being before, ahead, first, or forward. The headword reads Saqi, correcting OCR Siqi, and is distinct from the preceding physical-tip sense despite the identical spelling.
Saqiuo caquru is explained as going at the front in war. The Portuguese guerra visibly breaks after guer-; the q in the Japanese verb is retained rather than confused with g.
Completes guerra, then introduces competing for the leading position. The Japanese araſô has a circumflex and long s; the Portuguese object of contention follows on the next row.

Completes the contention over the lead, then introduces making someone go ahead. The Portuguese adiãteira keeps its nasal abbreviation and close initial join; the rounded initial v of voi is retained without changing the Japanese spelling.
Finishes “make someone go ahead” and introduces Saqini ſuſumu, advancing to the front. No extra paragraph sign is supplied before the new example, since the row proceeds directly into it.
Completes the advancing example as going or placing oneself in front. The long s in porſe and the wholly italic continuation are retained.

runs.text: O que corre, ou vai diante dalgũ

lines.note: Saqibaxiri denotes someone who runs or goes ahead of a lord. The nasal abbreviation is on the final u of dalgũ, not on a different vowel; the person's function continues below.

The advance runner serves as a lodging-arranger for a lord. A second, metaphorical use is introduced by Item; the paragraph sign belongs to the Portuguese apparatus and the description continues below.
The figurative meaning is a precursor or forerunner. The scan's close permet. is preserved rather than separated into a modernized Latin label; the long s in Precurſor is visible.

The compound means eating by tearing to pieces. Both supplied principal endings bear carons over o, and the Portuguese describes the same action; the old forms are not replaced with a modern conjugation.
Saqidachi first means going ahead, with the historical principal forms tçu and atta. The paragraph sign and abbreviated Itẽ introduce a figurative sense continued on the following row.

runs.text: permet. Morrer primeiro q̃ outro. Vt,

lines.note: The figurative sense is dying before another person. The printed q̃ abbreviation is not expanded, and italic Vt introduces Voyani, the start of an example about preceding one's parents in death.

runs.text: Morrer primeiro q̃ o pay, & mãy.

lines.note: Completes Voyani ſaqidatçu, explained as dying before father and mother. The Portuguese conjunction and comma remain literal; the nasal mark in mãy is preserved rather than modernizing the spelling.

The transitive entry means taking or putting something in front. The Portuguese couſa divides after cou, but the right-edge scan supplies no secure hyphen; none is added merely because the word continues.
Completes the literal placement definition and introduces putting reason first. Dǒriuo has a visible caron, and the Japanese example remains upright between two italic Portuguese runs.

runs.text: a razão diante, ou gouernarſe pella razão.

lines.note: The example is explained as carrying reason before oneself or governing oneself by reason. The long s in gouernarſe and the historical doubled l in pella are retained.

Saqigaqe denotes attacking or charging in front. Enlargement distinguishes the terminal baseline period from a higher spur on the adjacent right rule, correcting OCR's separated dash; the definition ends here and the next row is a new entry.
Saqigaqebayari describes eager or hurried initiative in charging. The Portuguese apreßado retains its double-s sort, and açodado visibly divides after aço- at the right margin.

runs.text: dado em arremeter a os inimigos. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the description as eagerness in charging the enemy and begins an example. The separated a os is retained, Vt is italic, and the Japanese form breaks at Saqi- before continuing below.

Completes Saqigaqe bayariuo ſuru, the action corresponding to the preceding eager-charge noun. The printed space before bayariuo and the long s in ſuru are retained; this whole continuation is Japanese and upright.
Saqigin denotes a vanguard or a body of troops going in front. The Portuguese esquadrão keeps the aligned short s; the location of the troop formation follows on the next row.
Completes the vanguard definition with “at the front.” The entire short continuation is italic and belongs to Saqigin, not to the following flowering verb.

The flowering-out verb is Saqijde: the comma-like shape after i is the surviving descender of a badly worn j. Faint upper traces and the supplied NINJAL Saqijde entry support this reading over OCR Saqi, de; the damaged j remains a nonblocking caveat. The example ends with ſaqi and no visible hyphen.
Completes Fanaga ſaqi izzuru and explains flowers coming out and sprouting. The doubled zz belongs to the historical verb form; the line starts with its continuation rather than a new headword.
Saqijei denotes the people or troops of the vanguard. The j in the Japanese compound is retained, and the Portuguese explanation is wholly italic.
The verb concerns abundant flowering. Its principal forms uru and eta are retained; the Portuguese alternative description continues after ou rather than ending the entry here.

runs.text: eſtarem as flores muito baſtas, & apinhoadas.

lines.note: The flowers are described as very dense and crowded together. The aligned provisional ſt spellings in eſtarem and baſtas are retained without imposing a global st-ligature reinterpretation; apinhoadas remains in the source spelling.
Saqimuxa identifies a soldier going in the vanguard. The Japanese x represents the historical spelling of the warrior element; it is not replaced by a modern sh sequence.
This adverbial expression means chiefly or principally. The headword is visibly close-joined as Saqitoxite, unlike the spaced example below; the grammatical label, definition and Vt are italic.

The example singles out this person in particular. Its printed spacing separates ſaqito and xite, and the Portuguese Principalmente begins the translation that continues below; no space is inserted into Conofitouo.
Completes the example as “principally this man.” The italic h has its local rounded form; the word is homem, not a new Japanese item or an entry boundary.

Saqi vma is a horse going ahead. The scan reads Cauallo, correcting OCR Cauillo, and keeps the space between the two Japanese words. The separate lower Saqi- is page furniture, not an extension of this definition.
